reading.rtitle: Complaint C-1188 -- what the customer is actually asking for
paras: The e-mail arrived at eight in the morning with four people in copy, and the first line is the one that matters: the order was promised for the twenty-fourth of May and it was delivered on the second of June. Nine days. He does not spend a single sentence on how he feels about it. He spends four sentences on what those nine days did to him, because that is the part he expects somebody to understand.

What they did to him is this. He had to call four of his own stores and tell them the product was not coming. One of those stores had a promotion running that week, with the product in the local advertising, so he paid for advertising that sent customers to an empty shelf. Another one gave the space to a competing brand and has not given it back. He writes all of that without one exclamation mark, which is usually the sign of somebody who is not shouting because he is deciding.

Then, halfway down, comes the sentence most people read too fast. I am not writing about a refund. He repeats it, in the last paragraph, in different words: money is not the problem here. Although he does mention the freight cost once, he never asks for it back. What he asks for is written twice, in both paragraphs, and it is the same thing: he wants to know what actually went wrong, and what has changed, so that he can tell his own team it will not happen again.

That is what makes this complaint worth answering carefully. A customer who wants money is asking for a transaction. A customer who wants an explanation is asking whether he can keep betting on you, and he has already decided that he would like to. The answer, therefore, has to contain three things and only three: the root cause, the corrective action, and a clear line about what is being given and what is not. However it is written, if it is missing the middle one, it is not an answer. It is an apology, and he did not ask for one.
reading.source: Internal case file -- key account, Midwest

gist.prompt: What is this customer actually asking for?
choices: A refund for the order and for the freight he paid
An explanation of the root cause and of what has changed, so he can defend the decision to keep buying
An apology from somebody senior in the company

items: The order was delivered nine days after the promised date.
The order was promised for the twenty-fourth of May and it was delivered on the second of June. Nine days.
One of his stores was running a promotion with the product in the local advertising.
One of those stores had a promotion running that week, with the product in the local advertising.
He asks for the freight cost to be returned.
Although he does mention the freight cost once, he never asks for it back.
He says twice that money is not what he is writing about.
I am not writing about a refund. He repeats it, in the last paragraph, in different words: money is not the problem here.
An answer with the cause and the gesture, but without the corrective action, is enough.
If it is missing the middle one, it is not an answer. It is an apology, and he did not ask for one.

listenings.text: Roberto, it is Dan Whitaker, seven thirty here, and I am going to say this on the phone because I do not want it to sound worse in writing than it is. The order landed on the second. It was promised for the twenty-fourth. That is nine days, and in those nine days I called four of my own stores and told them the product was not coming. One of them was running a promotion that week, with your product in the local paper, so I paid to send people to an empty shelf. Another one gave your space to somebody else and has not given it back yet. Now, listen, because this is the important part. I am not calling about a refund. I do not want your money. What I need, before I commit to the next order, is to know what actually went wrong and what has changed, because I have to say it out loud to my own team and I would like it to be true. Call me back.

I have written about a thousand of these, so let me save you the first five years. Rule one: acknowledge within twenty-four hours, always, even when you have absolutely no answer yet. And be clear about what acknowledging is. It is not agreeing, and it is not apologizing. It is saying: I received this, I have read it, I am working on it, and you will hear from me on this date. Rule two: a complete answer has exactly three parts. The root cause, in one sentence and without decoration. The corrective action, which is the change in the process that makes it impossible to repeat. And what you are giving, if you are giving anything. Most answers have the first and the third and skip the middle one, and the middle one is the only part that has any value to a professional buyer. Rule three, and this one costs companies money every single week: if you give something, name it as a goodwill gesture, out loud, in the letter. If you do not, the customer will assume you owed it, and next time he will expect it as a right.
